title: Are the roti shares 2 among 3, 4 among 6 and 6 among 9 the same?
description: Two rotis among three children, four rotis among six children and six rotis among nine children are compared. Each bigger group is made of copies of the first group, so the shares match, while Keeko doubts it because the numbers differ.
teaching_notes: One idea: a bigger sharing group made of copies of a smaller group gives the same share. Watch for students who think different numbers always mean different shares.

source: Equally divide the rotis and write down the share of each ch
video_script.why: The child writes the share of each child in three roti groups and explains why the shares are the same, because each bigger group is copies of the first group.
video_script.substitution: none: the book's own rotis shared among 3, 6 and 9 children
video_script.anchor: three mats: two rotis with three children, four rotis with six children, six rotis with nine children
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the shares are different, because the fractions have different numbers. Different numbers can still name the same amount, as halves showed, so we look at how the bigger groups are built.
video_script.payoff_line: The shares are the same, because each bigger group is copies of the first group

final_answer.value: a. 2/3; b. 4/6; c. 6/9. Yes, the shares are the same: 4 rotis among 6 children is two copies of 2 rotis among 3 children, and 6 among 9 is three copies, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9.
final_answer.spoken: two thirds, four sixths and six ninths, and yes, the shares are the same

video_script.fraction_reading: two thirds, four sixths, six ninths
maths_rules: (a) 2 rotis among 3 children: each child gets 2 ÷ 3 = 2/3
(b) 4 rotis among 6 children is 2 copies of (2 rotis, 3 children): each child still gets 2/3, written 4/6
(c) 6 rotis among 9 children is 3 copies of (2 rotis, 3 children): each child still gets 2/3, written 6/9
slip: Keeko thinks the shares are different because the numbers 4, 6, 9 differ
video_script.design: One idea: a bigger group is copies of the smaller group. The first group stays on the board and is copied twice and then three times.

beats.on_screen: Answer: a. 2/3; b. 4/6; c. 6/9. Yes, the shares are the same: 4 rotis among 6 children is two copies of 2 rotis among 3 children, and 6 among 9 is three copies, so 2/3 = 4/6 = 6/9.
